claims.statement: Maridebart cafraglutide (MariTide) is a bispecific molecule combining a monoclonal antibody antagonist of the GIP receptor (GIPR) with two conjugated GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonist peptides, designed to act as a GLP-1R agonist and GIPR antagonist simultaneously; its long antibody half-life is intended to support monthly or less-frequent dosing.

extractedEvidence.quote: bispecific glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIPR) antagonist
monthly or less frequent single-injection administration

claims.statement: Maridebart cafraglutide is an investigational drug with no FDA-approved indication as of the packet date; Amgen is running a Phase 3 program (MARITIME-1 in adults with overweight/obesity without type 2 diabetes; MARITIME-2 in adults with overweight/obesity and type 2 diabetes, plus additional studies planned across cardiovascular, heart-failure, kidney-disease, and obstructive-sleep-apnea populations) to generate the evidence regulators require before any approval decision.

context.formulation: investigational biologic, not a marketed product

claims.statement: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial (11 dose-arms across an obesity cohort of 465 participants and an obesity-with-type-2-diabetes cohort of 127 participants), mean percent body-weight change at the primary endpoint ranged from -12.3% to -16.2% with maridebart cafraglutide versus -2.5% with placebo in the obesity-only cohort, and from -8.4% to -12.3% versus -1.7% with placebo in the obesity-plus-diabetes cohort; glycated hemoglobin fell 1.2-1.6 percentage points with active drug versus 0.1 with placebo in the diabetes cohort.

context.population: adults with obesity (n=465), and adults with obesity/overweight plus type 2 diabetes (n=127)
context.doseText: 140, 280, or 420 mg every 4 weeks, or 420 mg every 8 weeks, with varying dose-escalation schedules (trial protocol only; not a use recommendation)

claims.statement: The Phase 2 trial protocol evaluated maridebart cafraglutide at 140, 280, or 420 mg administered subcutaneously every 4 weeks (and 420 mg every 8 weeks in the obesity-only cohort), with several dose-escalation schedules tested specifically to reduce gastrointestinal tolerability issues; this is trial-protocol context only, not a dosing recommendation, and there is no approved or labeled dose because the product is not FDA-approved.

claims.statement: In the Phase 2 trial, gastrointestinal adverse events (nausea, vomiting, constipation) were the most common adverse events with maridebart cafraglutide, described as generally less frequent with dose escalation and a lower starting dose; nausea and vomiting were predominantly mild, transient, and mostly associated with the first dose. Amgen reported a discontinuation rate of approximately 11% due to any adverse event in the dose-escalation arms, with less than 8% of discontinuations attributable to GI-related events, and stated no unexpected/additional safety signals were identified.

claims.statement: Published human evidence for maridebart cafraglutide is currently limited to a single Phase 2 dose-ranging trial with a 52-week primary endpoint; there is no completed Phase 3 evidence, no long-term (multi-year) safety or weight-maintenance data, no cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial data, and no FDA safety/efficacy determination. Popular online content already cites the Phase 2 percentages as though they were established, approved-product performance; this should not be treated as proof of long-term efficacy or safety in a general population.
